name: Lena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lena, 58. I've worked thirty years for the Hartley family at Westmoor, a 600-acre farm with 250 dairy cows, some beef and arable. I do the calving and rear the young stock. My husband Karl drives the school bus on the council contract. Our son Erik is a mechanic at the tractor dealer, and our daughter Ingrid is home with three little ones. We've a small terraced house in the village with a mortgage that ends when I'm 62.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the calf shed by half six, feeding sixty calves by bucket and teat. Then it's checking the cows due to calve, moving heifers, and the endless washing of buckets. Old Mr Hartley still comes round with his stick, and his son James runs it now. I love a calf on its feet within the hour. What wears me out is the cold, and the fact that we're always about three weeks from empty. I use the herd app on my phone that tells you which cows are coming into heat, and it's good, I'll give it that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So, all that fuss and not much change. That's usually how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say in the choir and at the shop that it's a lot of noise about nothing much. I'd say the herd app is useful, but it doesn't calve a cow. That's about my level of public opinion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel fairly safe at Westmoor. The Hartleys have kept me through two bad years. The worry is the money, not the job: three weeks saved, the mortgage still going, and Karl's bus contract up for renewal next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd put my overtime from calving season into the savings, maybe £60 a week from February to April. And I'd ask Karl to talk to the council early about the bus contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A little nag in the back about Karl's contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Karl's contract isn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then he'd look for driving for the haulier in town, which means early starts and less pay. We'd manage on my wage for a few months, but not long. Ingrid's husband Paul might help, but I'd hate to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you trust the Hartleys?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Hartley paid my wage the winter I broke my ankle, when he didn't have to. You don't forget that. James is cut from the same cloth, mostly.

say: I'd say at choir and the shop it's **a lot of noise** about little.
I'd say the herd app is useful but **doesn't calve a cow**.
think: My **job feels safe** because the Hartleys have kept me through bad years.
The worry is **money**: three weeks saved and Karl's bus contract up next summer.
do: Save my **calving overtime**, about £60 a week from February to April.
Ask Karl to raise the **bus contract** with the council early.
Keep **rearing calves** at Westmoor as usual.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a nag about **Karl's contract**.
S0.quote: Old Mr Hartley paid my wage the winter I broke my ankle, when he didn't have to. You don't forget that.
fieldNote: Her **loyalty to the Hartleys** gives her a sense of job security.
The household worry is **her husband's contract**, not her own work.
She's a light, contented **app user** who still values the hands-on part most.

steps.text: Save calving-season overtime, about £60 a week
Keep rearing the sixty calves at Westmoor as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying and answering. That's James's office mostly. The calf shed's hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible for the farm to use what works, as long as it doesn't push good people out. I'd say that to James if he asked. I'd not go shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm fine for a few years. James will use AI for the feed orders and the milk records, and maybe the herd app gets cleverer. The calves still need hands. But I'd watch the dairy robots, because the big farms already have milking robots and James has looked at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the herd app properly, all of it, the health alerts and the calf weights, once James sets it up and the others are using it. I'd keep working as I am. And I'd keep saving the calving money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but not scared. It's like a new bull in the field, you keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if James brought in milking robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well done, if it keeps the farm going, and I'd mean it. Milking robots take the milkers' jobs, not mine, but I'd feel for Piotr and Agnes. They've young families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about Erik's work at the dealer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik will be fine, he fixes the things. My son Erik says every robot that comes in needs a man with a spanner and a laptop. I hope he's right.

say: I'd say the farm should **use what works**, if good people aren't pushed out.
I'd say it to James if asked, **not shout** about it.
think: The **calves still need hands** for a few years yet.
I'd watch for **milking robots**, which James has already looked at.
do: Learn the **herd app** fully once James sets it up.
Keep **working as usual** in the calf shed.
Keep saving the **calving money** each spring.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like watching a **new bull** in the field.
S1.quote: My son Erik says every robot that comes in needs a man with a spanner and a laptop.
fieldNote: She expects the **office side** to change first and her calf work to stay.
Her concern is for **the milkers**, Piotr and Agnes, rather than herself.
Typical steady approach: **learn the app** once others are using it.

steps.text: Learn the herd app's health alerts and calf weights
Keep rearing calves by hand in the Westmoor calf shed
Save the calving overtime again this spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028, and robots by 2031. I'd be 63. The mortgage would be done, just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for ordinary families, and the people in charge should think of the villages. I'd say it at church and at the school gate when I pick up the grandchildren. I'd not march, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the AI in 2028 runs James's office, and he'll see the numbers on robots straight away. By 2031 a robot can feed calves and check heifers, and James would have to buy one or go under. Loyalty or not, he'd have to. I'd likely be gone at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd talk to James properly about what he plans, so I'm not surprised. I'd ask whether I could learn to run the calf robots, if he gets them. I'd offer to childmind Ingrid's three for a bit of money if I lost the job. And Karl and I would stop the holiday fund and put it in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And sad, because it wouldn't be the Hartleys' fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to James?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, James, I don't want charity, I want honesty. Tell me a year ahead. He would. His father would have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd childmind. Would that pay enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not near my wage. But Ingrid could go back to work at the bakery, and that's money in the family. That's how my mother's family got through the bad years.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for ordinary families and villages.
I'd say it at **church** and the school gate, but not march.
think: AI in 2028 shows James **the robot numbers** straight away.
By 2031 he'd have to buy robots, and I'd likely be **gone at 63**.
do: Ask James directly about his **plans** for the calf shed.
Ask to learn the **calf robots** if he buys them.
Stop the **holiday fund** and save it instead.
feel: **Alarmed**, and **sad** because it wouldn't be the Hartleys' fault.
S2.quote: I'd say, James, I don't want charity, I want honesty. Tell me a year ahead.
fieldNote: She doesn't **blame her employer**; she sees him forced by the market.
Her fallback is **family**: childminding so her daughter can work.
Short warning puts robots in calf rearing at **age 63**, before her pension.

steps.text: Ask James Hartley for a year's notice of any robot plans
Ask to learn the calf-feeding robots if Westmoor buys them
Childmind Ingrid's three so she can return to the bakery
Stop the holiday fund and move it into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. I'd be 66. That's not long before I'd stop anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning, so families and farms should plan together. I'd say young people should learn from older ones while there's time. That's how I'd put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right, just about. The mortgage is done at 62, the AI comes in 2031, and James plans the robots then, maybe for 2034. I'd only lose the last year before my pension, and I could live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the herd system properly, once the others are on it. I'd pay a bit extra on the mortgage to clear it a year early. And I'd wait to see what James decides before worrying out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a road I can see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Westmoor in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnes, who milks. She's forty with two boys and she's good, but she's no other trade. I'd tell her to ask James for the robot training first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only lose a year. Would that year be a problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would be thin, with Karl's bus money and nothing else. But we'd have no mortgage. A house with no mortgage is a house you can be poor in safely.

say: I'd say five years is **fair warning**, so families and farms should plan together.
I'd say young people should **learn from older ones** while there's time.
think: With the **mortgage done at 62**, I'd likely just about manage.
I'd only lose the **last year** before my pension.
do: Learn the **herd system** once the others use it.

feel: **Anxious** but **steady**, seeing the end of the road.
S3.quote: A house with no mortgage is a house you can be poor in safely.
fieldNote: Her anchor is the **mortgage end date**, which comes before robots in this case.
She'd still face a **thin year** before her pension on Karl's wage alone.
She thinks of a younger colleague, **Agnes**, and would steer her to robot training.

steps.text: Learn the full herd system once others are using it
Overpay the mortgage to finish it a year early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. I'd be 71. I'd be retired, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a farm like Westmoor to do it right, and to keep its people. I'd say it to James and in the village. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm out of it. The mortgage is gone, I retire at 67, and the robots come later. The worry is the usual one, the thin savings and Karl's contract. And Ingrid's little ones, who'll grow up in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am. I'd help Erik if he wants to set up on his own fixing farm robots, maybe with a bit of the savings. And I'd teach my granddaughter Mia to bottle-feed a calf, so she knows where milk comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the ordinary kind. Not about robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really put savings into Erik's business with three weeks in the bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, a few hundred maybe, and only once the mortgage is done. But family helps family. Erik would pay it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will anything be lost when robots rear calves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The talking. I talk to every calf. A robot will feed the calves right, but nobody will tell them they're a good girl.

say: I'd say ten years is enough for farms like Westmoor to **keep their people**.
I'd say it **quietly**, to James and in the village.
think: I retire at 67, **before the robots**, with the mortgage gone.
The usual worries remain: **thin savings** and Karl's contract.
do: Keep **working** in the calf shed until retirement.
Help son Erik start a **farm robot repair** business with a few hundred pounds.
Teach granddaughter Mia to **bottle-feed** a calf.
feel: **Uneasy** in the ordinary way, not about robots.
S4.quote: A robot will feed the calves right, but nobody will tell them they're a good girl.
fieldNote: Ten years means robots arrive **after her retirement**; old money worries remain.
She'd back her son's **robot repair** idea within the family.
Her sense of loss is about **care and talk**, not jobs.

steps.text: Keep rearing calves at Westmoor until retiring at 67
Lend son Erik a few hundred pounds for a robot repair business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. The robots would arrive at 63, before my pension, and James would have no choice. What would help is employers giving honest notice, and families being able to help each other, like childminding counting for something. Not more government forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old farmers. Mr Hartley is 84 and still walks the yard. Nobody asks what a farm means to the old ones who built it.

headlineQuote: Mr Hartley is 84 and still walks the yard. Nobody asks what a farm means to the old ones who built it.
portrait: Lena, 58, has reared calves for thirty years on the **Hartley family's dairy farm**.
Her husband drives the school bus; they have **thin savings** and a mortgage ending at 62.
She uses the herd app now and then and would **learn more** once others do.
She trusts the **Hartleys**, doesn't blame them, and leans on **family** for support.
She's **alarmed** with two years' warning, anxious with five and uneasy with ten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots arriving at **63**, before her pension.
whatWouldHelp: Recognising **family help** like childminding, not more government forms.
